content.thinking:
This piece is a "how climate science works" methods-style text, heavy on rigor and evidence with vivid details like ice cores and the ink-in-swimming-pool analogy. It mostly targets the competence dimension of trust rather than benevolence or integrity, with no messenger presence or acknowledgment of counterarguments, so I'd expect a modest trust gain, maybe around +1.9 on the multidimensional scale.

For the individual outcomes, I'm estimating small positive shifts across the board: trust_post around +1.2, distrust around -1.0, funding perceptions and policy role each around +0.9-1.1 given mentions of assessments and NASA satellites, belief around +0.8, concern around +0.6, and diminishing effects further down to policy_general (+0.45), policy_specific (+0.35), behavior (+0.25), donation (+0.05), and newsletter signup (+0.006) — this being one of several similar "Measurement & modeling" arms in the study.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a purely expository account of how climate science is done — instruments, ice cores, isotopes, satellites, models — with some vivid concreteness (volcanic ash fingerprints, 'a drop of ink in an Olympic pool'). Its mechanism is competence/epistemic-rigor signaling: it should raise the competence subscale most, openness somewhat (methods transparency), and integrity/benevolence only indirectly, so the four-subscale primary index gets a diluted, moderate boost (~+2). There is no ideologically congruent messenger, no correction of a misperception, no acknowledgment of criticism or funding issues, so it lacks the counter-attitudinal punch of source-credibility or inoculation arms; it is also long and somewhat dry, which caps engagement. Downstream outcomes get progressively smaller effects: re-asked single items (trust_post, belief_post) are shrunk by pre-treatment anchoring; the explicit NASA/satellite and 'findings inform international assessments' content gives small positive nudges to institutional trust and the scientists-in-policy items; mentions of heatwaves/droughts/flooding give only a slight concern bump. Policy support and behavioral intentions are distal and near-zero-to-small, and the incentivized measures (AMS donation, newsletter signup) should move only a few cents / a fraction of a percentage point, though the meteorology-science framing marginally favors the AMS donation.
